final_recommendation: The room converged on a protocol amendment with binding labor enforcement: Mexico commits to 48-hour auditor access to facilities named in complaints, with automatic tariff snapback on day 31 if access is refused or blocked. Canada supports if the amendment stays labor-only (Chapter 23). Congress demands mid-January vote with clear enforcement language to secure caucus support.
minority_objections: Labor union initially demanded mandatory day-31 tariff snapback with no Mexico remedy choice, which Canada and Mexico resisted as too punitive and risking reopening other chapters
key_conflicts: Congress vs. Mexico on whether tariff snapback should be automatic-on-refusal vs. mandatory-regardless-of-good-faith-negotiation
Labor union's demand for mandatory tariffs vs. Mexico's insistence on preserving remedy choice to maintain sovereignty
Business lobby's mid-January vote deadline vs. Congress's need for caucus buy-in on enforcement language
key_concessions: Mexico accepted real-time auditor access during 30-day review and 48-hour facility access trigger
Congress accepted Mexico's remedy choice (remediation vs. tariffs) as long as snapback is automatic on refusal/blocking
Canada accepted labor enforcement amendment in exchange for explicit text limiting changes to Chapter 23 only
red_lines: Canada: no reopening of dairy, Chapter 19, or other chapters beyond labor enforcement
Mexico: no mandatory tariffs if participating in good faith; snapback only on refusal/blocking
Congress: no vote without automatic snapback trigger and real-time auditor visibility during review
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Trade lawyer's warning about future disputes over 'organizing sites only' investigator access boundaries was acknowledged but not resolved in detail
Media actor's concern about public narrative clarity ('binding enforcement' vs. 'Mexico gets to remediate first') was raised repeatedly but the final messaging remained somewhat ambiguous
Potential for Mexico to claim 'still preparing access' and trigger interpretation disputes, though lawyer attempted to close this with day-3 automatic trigger language
downstream_risk_variables: Whether 15 holdout Congress members accept the 48-hour + day-31 snapback language as sufficient enforcement teeth
Whether Mexico's domestic politics can absorb the sovereignty concession of 48-hour auditor access without triggering backlash
Whether Canada's dairy-protection red line holds if other parties attempt to reopen chapters post-amendment
Whether business lobby's mid-January timeline is realistic given remaining caucus uncertainty
Whether labor activists accept the final package as a 'real win' or continue to pressure for mandatory tariffs
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved procedural convergence on amendment mechanics (48-hour access, day-31 snapback on refusal) but left unresolved: (1) the exact public messaging to labor activists and Congress members on whether this is 'binding enforcement' or 'Mexico-first remediation'; (2) whether the 15 holdout Congress members will actually vote yes; (3) how Mexico will defend the sovereignty concession domestically; (4) whether the mid-January vote timeline is achievable given remaining caucus work.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress opened with 'we're dead on arrival' without enforcement, repeatedly stated 'the votes aren't there' and '15 members won't move unless...', driving every round toward amendment
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor union demanded facility inspections, tariff snapback, investigator access in R1; escalated to mandatory day-31 snapback in R4; shaped every compromise on enforcement mechanics
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business lobby pushed mid-January vote deadline and certainty (R2, R4) but was not the dominant driver—enforcement mechanics took precedence over business timeline concerns
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada set clear red line ('no reopening dairy/Chapter 19') in R1-R3 and conditioned support on labor-only amendment, but this was a boundary condition rather than a driving force
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico resisted 'U.S. policing' and 'too broad' auditor access in R1-R2, insisted on remedy choice and participation-based triggers, but ultimately accepted 48-hour access—concern was real but yielded to enforcement pressure
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor repeatedly demanded 'one clean sentence' for public narrative and warned about labor activist skepticism, but this was framing pressure rather than a decision driver
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: The entire meeting treated the original package as unratifiable ('dead on arrival') and structured all discussion around what amendment would make ratification viable—stability explicitly contingent on amendment
